summary: Radar Absheron is a mobile-first, bilingual (English and Azerbaijani) interactive story map and radar explorer built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. It translates complex L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission into plain-language insights for farmers, water managers, students, and citizens across Baku, the Absheron Peninsula, and the semi-arid Kura-Araz lowland.In Azerbaijan, 92% of freshwater goes to agriculture and 63% of cropland is irrigated, with the largest share concentrated in the Kura-Araz lowland. While optical satellites like MODIS are blocked by cloud cover and darkness, NISAR sees through clouds day and night every 12 days. However, raw SAR metrics are unreadable to non-experts, and no localized Azerbaijani tools exist. Radar Absheron bridges this gap with a 9-step visual story, an interactive 15-pass time-series map, and tap-to-explain agricultural guidance-turning complex radar backscatter into actionable water and surface-change intelligence.
details:
Radar Absheron is an open-source, mobile-first bilingual (Azerbaijani and English) interactive story map and radar explorer that translates NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data into plain-language insights for everyone in Azerbaijan.

What It Does & How It Works:

Unlike optical satellites (such as NASA Terra/MODIS) that depend on sunlight and are blocked by clouds, NISAR transmits its own L-band radio waves to observe ground and water conditions through clouds, day and night, every 12 days. Radar Absheron turns these complex measurements into an accessible web experience with two core modes:

9-Step Guided Story ("The Dance"):

Walks users through how radar sees through clouds, how to read color composites, how the land responds to rainfall, how wind roughens the Caspian Sea, why urban Baku stays stable, and how multi-pass change detection works. Every step opens with an everyday "In short" summary, with technical explanations (dB, HH/HV polarizations, σ° backscatter) available in one tap.

Interactive Explorer:

Lets users scrub across 15 NISAR passes (June-October 2026), drag a swipe slider to compare cloudy NASA MODIS true-color photos against clear NISAR radar views from the exact same morning (such as 12 July 2026), and tap any location to view its backscatter history and practical agricultural guidance.

Scientific Validation:

Cross-checking NISAR observations against independent NASA measurements across 15 passes confirmed measurable physical signals: following ~12-18 mm of rainfall on 3 October 2026 (NASA POWER), median land soil moisture rose from 0.18 to 0.23 m³/m³ and radar backscatter increased by +0.6 to +1.3 dB above stable urban, oil-field, and sea controls, while Caspian Sea brightness correlated strongly with hourly wind speed (r = 0.63).

Benefits & Intended Impact:

In Azerbaijan, 92% of freshwater goes to agriculture and 63% of cropland is irrigated, with the largest share concentrated in the semi-arid Kura-Araz lowland. Radar Absheron delivers three main benefits:

For farmers and agronomists: Cloud-free visibility into wet or dry ground after rainfall across ~6,600 km² of irrigated farmland.

For water managers: Basin-wide monitoring across the entire Kura-Araz lowland every 12 days rather than relying solely on isolated field visits.

For schools and universities: The first Azerbaijani-language radar remote sensing resource built with local data.

Because our open-source processing pipeline is fully scripted, it can automatically refresh after every 12-day NISAR pass, scale across all of Azerbaijan and irrigated basins in the South Caucasus and Central Asia, and incorporate 10-20 m GCOV products for field-level crop and flood mapping at near-zero running cost.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used:

Data & APIs: NASA-ISRO NISAR Level-3 Soil Moisture (NISAR L3 SME2, PROVISIONAL, doi:10.5067/NIL3SME2-P1) and calibrated HH/HV backscatter (σ°, dB) via ASF DAAC; NASA POWER precipitation and hourly wind speed; NASA Terra/MODIS and Blue Marble via NASA GIBS.

Web & Mapping Stack:

Lightweight static web application built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and the Leaflet mapping library, deployed openly on GitHub Pages ([https://suathamzali.github.io/radar-absheron](https://www.google.com/search?q=https://suathamzali.github.io/radar-absheron)) with open-source code on GitHub ([https://github.com/suathamzali/radar-absheron](https://www.google.com/search?q=https://github.com/suathamzali/radar-absheron)).

Processing & Hardware:

Reproducible open-source data processing and validation scripts (testing rain, wind, cloud cover, urban controls, and NDVI irrigation masks) executed on a single standard laptop using free NASA archives.

Creativity & Key Factors:

Creativity ("Legend First, Then Data"):

Rather than assuming technical expertise, the interface teaches users what radar colors represent before asking them to read a map, framing multi-pass radar data as a physical "dance" where the sea moves with the wind, the land reacts to the rain, and the city acts as a steady anchor.

Scientific Honesty:

All imagery is calibrated on one fixed dB scale using urban Baku as a control baseline, paired with noise-floor warnings, "provisional" data labels, and transparent reporting of resolution limits (noting that while regional soil moisture shifts are clear at 200 m-1 km, single-field monitoring requires NISAR's 10-20 m resolution product).

Accessibility & Rural Usability:

Built phone-first with zero installation required, tested across 1280 px, 375 px, and 320 px viewports in both Azerbaijani and English, and engineered with full keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, and reduced-motion options.
